As such, this course requires the completion of two or more substantial writing assignments or the equivalent. Instructors will provide criteria for evaluating your performance on writing, feedback on your writing (including instructor response), and opportunities for revision.
By the end of this course, undergraduate students will be able to:
Compose ideas clearly, coherently, and effectively for a particular purpose, occasion, or audience representative as appropriate for the field.
Develop an intelligence report using the industry standard plain-language in a message-driven format
Evaluate appropriate evidence from multiple sources to illustrate how a chosen topic is relevant to a particular field.
Evaluate intelligence analyses based on characteristics and industry measurements
Explain the ethical dilemmas surrounding intelligence collection and analysis
Identify challenges in the current intelligence community within the scope of analytical functions
In order to fulfill FSU’s Scholarship in Practice requirement, the student must earn a “C-” or higher in the course.

In order to fulfill FSU’s Upper-Division Writing requirement, the student must earn a “C-” or higher in the course, and earn at least a “C-” average on the required writing assignments. If the student does not earn a “C-” average or better on the required writing assignments, the student will not earn an overall grade of “C-” or better in the course, no matter how well the student performs in the remaining portion of the course.

In this course, you will compose as a process, including drafts, revisions, and editing. The writing cultivated by this process conforms to FSU’s definition of “college-level writing”, which is writing that:
is organized clearly and logically;
is presented in a format appropriate to the purpose, occasion, and audience; and
Operationalize, measure, and model intelligence based on quantitative data
Prepare analyses and reports on both target and mission-specific topics
presents a clearly defined central idea or thesis;
provides adequate support for that idea;
Synthesize tactical analyses and reports on both target and mission-specific topics

The Semester Intelligence Project (SIP) consists of four (4) deliverables. Each deliverable will build on previous analyst work, culminating in a group briefing at the end of the semester. The SIP is designed to lead the student analyst through the entirety of the intelligence cycle, illustrating key concepts and methodology along the way.
This project will require significant effort on the part of student analysts - plan for that.

There are hard requirements throughout the SIP, with harsh but realistic penalties associated with these. In the real world, an unsatisfactory product will not receive a poor grade; it will simply be discarded. Analysts are cautioned to understand the ‘no-go’ criteria for each portion of the SIP.

Throughout this project, students will use ICD 203/ISD 203-1 citations. This is the same format used and required by the U.S. Intelligence Community, and will prepare students for work in the field (or similar areas). This format is not used in academia and will be discussed in a course lecture.

Topics will be assigned to student analysts in week 2 of the semester. Student analysts will be randomly divided into Analyst Teams. The Analyst Teams will each have a SIP topic assigned, and all student analysts in that team will work on the same broad topic.
The SIP is an individual effort - each analyst will produce independent work.
The Final Briefing (delivered in class) is a combined effort of the Analyst Team. Each student analyst will contribute to the Final Briefing and participate in the classroom presentation.
The four (4) Deliverables are:

l: Semester Intelligence Project (SIP) 2 Collection and Qualitative Analysis

p: At the end of the semester, students will present their work as part of their assigned group.

This assignment is the first step in completing the Semester Intelligence Project. The purpose is to ensure that the student analyst understands the assigned topic and is prepared to proceed through the remainder of the project.

This assignment is two-fold. The first portion will develop the student analyst’s assigned topic, laying the foundation for the SIP. The second portion will discuss implicit and explicit analyst bias and is critical to the integrity of the entire SIP.
The student will prepare a brief paper with two major sections.

l: Section 1: The student will prepare a high-level background of the assigned topic and focus on how their project will address the intelligence questions.
p: This assignment is similar to an academic research paper. The student analyst must discuss any background information that is significant to the topic assigned and associated intelligence questions. The analyst should present a solid amount of research and support on the assigned topic. Some questions to consider when writing your background:
How has the topic developed in recent months or years? What are the origins of the topic? Is there significant historical information required for understanding?
Why should decision makers care about the topic and the product that the analyst will develop this semester?
What is happening that concerns the topic currently? Are there potential bad outcomes?
Are there any internal or external factors that influence the topic?
Is there ANYTHING else that may interest the target audience?

l: Section 2: The student analyst will produce a discussion of their biases and how they will be accounted for in research and writing throughout the SIP.
p: This methodology should apply to this assignment and to all future work on this topic. This assessment of bias should focus on the assigned topic and include both explicit and implicit bias concerns. The goal is for the student analyst to understand where bias issues may arise, acknowledge them, and clearly define how those issues will be minimized. Intelligence and analytical products should always include this component.
Student analysts should provide examples of bias (either explicit or implicit) and cited sources that indicate effective research on how these biases may impact writing.
Some of the questions that the product should answer are:
How could biases influence the field of intelligence?
What are some common biases that may be linked to your topic?
How are some of these common biases presented?
How can biases in the media sway public opinion on your assigned topic?
What are your biases? Everyone is biased.
What steps will the analyst take to account for bias?

The student analyst will make an acknowledgement of any personal biases they may have about the assigned topic and the steps that they have taken to mitigate these. The analyst must be upfront here. The goal is for the instructors to clearly understand how the analyst will provide a final product that is unbiased.
The student analyst must not use first-person language. Statements such as “I will…” should be rephrased as “The analyst has…”, etc. This applies to the entire Semester Intelligence Project.
This second section does not require citations, but the analyst may utilize cited information as necessary.
The submission should be between 900-1200 words (for undergraduates) or 1200-1500 words (for graduates), double-spaced, 12pt, Times New Roman or Calibri font.
The body should be fairly evenly split between the background content and the bias content.
Endnote citations are required. All citations must be in ICD 203/ICS 203-1 format.
The submission will include a title page.

The submission will include a header and a footer. The header must include the word count of the body of the submission, which does not include the abstract or endnotes. The footer must include a page number and analyst name.
The submission will include outside sources (in ICD endnote format) that support the statements made in the submission.

l: Semester Intelligence Project (SIP) 2 - Collection and Qualitative Analysis

p: This step requires the analyst to collect Publicly Available Information (PAI), Commercially Available Information (CAI), and Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) regarding the assigned topic and begin an analysis on the resulting dataset. Student analysts will use the template provided to collect the required information and structure the initial analysis.
The primary and recommended platform for this assignment is X.com (formerly Twitter). Student analysts are expected to create and utilize a free account to perform these actions.

Student analysts will use the social media application X to collect a sample of 75 posts on the assigned topic. Student analysts will use Search Strings and Operators to find and collect this sample data. Analysts will manually select applicable posts from search results and copy/paste the content of the post into the right column of the template document. It is recommended that the analyst collect all 75 posts first, before proceeding.

After the sample is collected and pasted into the right column, the analyst will then use highlighters (the highlighter tool in Word, for example) to code the data by theme. Using words or phrases in the post text, the analyst will identify and highlight segments of the post that indicate meaning or applicability to a theme, idea, or context. In the left column for that post, the analyst should enter a brief memo: a rationale or other reason that the post is being coded to a theme. When coding the post, the entirety of the post text should not be highlighted in one color. More than one theme can be highlighted/included in a post.

The posts that are collected should be a broad representation of the assigned topic. Using the bias discussion in SIP 1, remember that the collection, codes, and memos should all be free of implicit or explicit bias. It is acceptable to note the bias that may be present in a user’s post, but that should be based strictly on the content that is available in the post. For example, it is unacceptable to infer someone's political bias from their post or to assert that they may be left or right-leaning based on one statement. However, if the post says, “I am a republican OR democrat, and I think…” then it is fair to note their political leanings. If there is no explicit expression of their affiliations, the analyst cannot assume. This assignment does not require the analyst to dig into their profile to build a case. This assignment serves to capture information shared in singular tweets to get a brief snapshot of information that is associated with the assigned topic.

Memos can be any information that the analyst thinks is relevant to note about the post. Some of the collected posts may not contribute anything significant, but the product shouldn’t contain more than five (5) posts like that. All posts must include a memo.

The student analyst should use the template document provided in these instructions. Posts and memos should be in 12pt, Times New Roman or Calibri font. There should be between 3 and 5 different colors to code the information; these codes will be used later as themes in the written analysis. The themes identified must be original and cannot come from any examples provided in the course.

The codes must be defined by color in the product. The analyst must be clear about what each color means. For example, “Blue = In support of international intervention.” These codes can be defined above or below the collected post table.

The last page of the submission is the Search Strings and Operators utilized to collect these posts. Analysts should utilize a wide range of Search Strings and Operators; using one or two search strings will not give you a broad picture and is not acceptable.

Each Semester Intelligence Project (SIP) Group is correlated to an Intel Request below. You will all work individually throughout the semester, and then collaborate on a class briefing (presentation) at the end of the term.

Many of these request topics are very broad. You may go where your research takes you, while I am not going to specify a course of inquiry - there are some suggestions in the requests. Those suggestions are not all-encompassing but may help you start to brainstorm. Throughout the semester you will find the Semester Intelligence Project assignments start to focus your work.

For each of these assignments, assume you work for a contractor associated with an Intelligence Community member agency. Your task is deep background and analysis of OSINT and GEOINT - open source, publicly available information. You should include public perception and/or opinion about the topic - something that policy makers may take into account.
Your work does not require access to any material with any type of security classification. The description of the intel request for your group should help you focus your scope.

The United States is looking at potential courses of action for stabilizing the Venezuelan government. Your project should focus on mid-2025 and moving forward and should take into account the change of regime in Caracas. You should certainly investigate and discuss oil exports, narcotics trafficking, and linkages to other superpowers.

Yemen and its internal conflict continue to be a concern in the Red Sea region. The United States is looking for potential courses of action to ensure regional stability and freedom of trade in the area. Your product should include a discussion of US and allied military activity, as well as an explanation for the rise and persistence of the Houthis.

Cybersecurity and cybercrime are a critical threat to the United States. Your product should include information on The Com as well as similar or allied groups and be directed at decision makers who have little to no knowledge about the topic.

Unrest and violence in Rwanda have been a destabilizing factor in the region. The United States is looking to stabilize the area. Decision makers need a detailed report on the background and activities of M23 as well as potential future actions. Your product should include a discussion of the support received by M23, as well as their goals and objectives.

Sudan has been a concern on the African continent for decades. The United States is looking to increase its projection of power to bring stability to the region. Your report is aimed at decision-makers. You have little to no deep information about current conditions, historical trends, or future activities.

Despite the fall of the Assad regime, Syria remains a hotspot of violence. U.S. forces have been engaged in the region for a significant amount of time, and the United States is looking for potential courses of action that will result in increasing stability in Syria and the surrounding area. Your report should discuss Russian influence as well as regional powers such as Israel, and what their intent may be.

The border between Afghanistan and Pakistan, known as the Durand Line, is a hotly contested political line on a map. Your report is aimed at decision-makers who have no in-depth knowledge of the traditional cultural and tribal clashes created by this international border. The United States is looking for potential courses of action to stabilize the area, and decision-makers need in-depth background information.

All work in this course must be cited in accordance with ICD-206. There are almost no exceptions.

ICD 206 is the methodology utilized by the intelligence community to ensure readers of intelligence products understand where data and information is coming from. Within the intelligence community, citations are as critical (or more so) as they are in academia. This course reflects that. If you do not cite your work, you will likely receive a zero as a grade for that assignment.
